 Remote-Control Stunt Cars and Baby Teether Sets Recalled Two Weeks Before Black Friday Over Battery and Choking Hazards
 Published Nov 13, 2026 7:45 PM EST 
 By
 Elena Vega 
 Editorial Illustration via AI 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Two toys sold online have been recalled because they can seriously injure young children, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission announced Nov. 12, two weeks before the Black Friday shopping rush. A remote-controlled stunt car has batteries children can easily reach, and a baby rattle and teether set has parts that can break off and choke an infant.
 The Kakgold 4WD stunt vehicle recall covers about 294 units sold on Amazon. The SHEIN rattle and teether set recall covers about 2,657 sets. No injuries have been reported for either product, and both companies are offering refunds.
 The numbers are small, but the hazards are not. For parents and grandparents shopping for the holidays, the recalls are a reminder to check how a toy's batteries are secured and whether small pieces can come loose before it goes under the tree.
 Two Recalls, Two Ways a Toy Can Hurt a Child
 The Kakgold car has a lime green and blue body, a black chassis, and four black wheels with lime green trim. The body has checkered patterns, an "X" design, and the words "PRO" and "RACING," and a white hang tag reads "Do Not Twist the Shaft." It sold on Amazon from July through September 2026 for $34 to $50.
 The problem is in the remote control. It holds button cell and lithium-ion batteries that children can easily reach, a violation of the mandatory federal toy standard, the CPSC said. Owners should stop using the car, write "RECALLED" on it, and email a photo of it being thrown away to kakrecall@outlook.com for a full refund. The button cell batteries should be disposed of or recycled following local hazardous waste rules. The firm is Shenzhenshi Juteng Lechuang Technology Co., Ltd., doing business as Kakgold, of China.
 The SHEIN sets include seven toys in pastel colors and shapes. The purple and orange knobs can detach, creating a choking hazard, and because the sets are meant for children under 3, they violate the federal small parts ban. They were sold on US.Shein.com from November 2025 through July 2026 for about $10. The SKU sk25070936134444119 appears on a label on the packaging.
 Parents should take the sets away from children and contact SHEIN at 833-853-8668 or through the "Product Recalls" link at the bottom of US.Shein.com. Refunds require confirming the sets were thrown away.
 Neither recall says how many toys have been returned so far. Because both products resemble many similar items sold online, parents can compare the descriptions with their order history before throwing anything away.
 Hours, Not Days: The Button Battery Danger
 A swallowed button battery can lodge in a child's esophagus and burn through tissue. "Severe damage can occur in just 2 hours," according to the National Capital Poison Center . Children may show few symptoms at first, and even a used battery can cause injury.
 The CPSC has warned that "the ingested batteries can cause serious injuries, internal chemical burns and death," as it said in an earlier battery toy recall . Federal rules adopted under Reese's Law require battery compartments on consumer products to be secured so children cannot easily open them.
 Battery injuries have climbed over time. A study in Pediatrics estimated 70,322 battery-related emergency visits among U.S. children from 2010 to 2019, more than double the number from 1990 to 2009, with button batteries involved in about 85%, AuntMinnie reported . Children under 5 were at highest risk, especially toddlers ages 1 and 2.
 Toddlers and preschoolers are at the greatest risk because they explore with their mouths. Older siblings who take toys apart and grandparents' homes that may not be childproofed add to the exposure. Batteries can also be pushed into a child's nose or ear .
 Babies and toddlers also face the choking risk from small parts. Anything that fits inside a toilet paper tube is small enough to block a young child's airway.
 Steps if a Child Swallows a Battery or Chokes
 Parents should not wait for symptoms if they think a child swallowed a battery. The Poison Center advises calling the 24-hour National Battery Ingestion Hotline at 1-800-498-8666 right away and going to the emergency room if advised. An X-ray is usually needed. Bringing the battery package or a matching battery helps doctors.
 If the battery was swallowed within the past 12 hours and the child can swallow, the Poison Center advises giving 2 teaspoons of honey every 10 minutes on the way to the emergency room. Honey should never delay care, and it should not be given to babies younger than 1.
 Warning signs can include drooling, gagging, trouble swallowing, refusing food, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever or blood in the stool. A missing battery or an opened remote is reason enough to seek care, even if the child seems fine.
 A child who is choking and cannot cry, cough, or breathe needs immediate help. Call 911 and, if trained, use back blows and chest thrusts for infants or abdominal thrusts for older children.
 Holiday Shopping With Safety in Mind
 Shoppers can look for toys with battery compartments that need a screwdriver to open and avoid toys with small detachable parts for children under 3. Checking the recall list at CPSC.gov before buying, especially for low-cost toys from online marketplaces, takes only a minute. Spare and used button batteries should be stored up high, and dead batteries should be taped and recycled promptly. Problems with any toy can be reported at SaferProducts.gov. MedicalDaily will report on further toy recalls before the holidays.

 Key Questions Answered
 Which toys were recalled? Kakgold 4WD remote-controlled stunt cars sold on Amazon and SHEIN baby rattle and teether sets sold on US.Shein.com.
 What are the hazards? The car's remote has batteries children can easily reach. The teether sets have knobs that can detach and cause choking.
 Is there a refund? Yes. Kakgold and SHEIN are both offering refunds after owners confirm disposal.
 What should I do if my child swallows a battery? Call the National Battery Ingestion Hotline at 1-800-498-8666 right away and go to the emergency room if advised.
 Can I give honey? For a child older than 1 who can swallow and swallowed a battery within 12 hours, the Poison Center advises honey on the way to the emergency room. Never delay care for it.
 Has anyone been hurt? No injuries have been reported for either product.
